course.title: Clio: Your Terminal Assistant
course.description: Learn to use Clio — the offline-first CLI assistant that turns plain English into shell commands. Built for Termux and Nigerian students who want to code on their phone without memorizing Linux syntax.
course.objectives: Install Clio, ask questions in plain English, run setup wizards, download automation modules, and work confidently on Termux.
course.prerequisites: Basic familiarity with opening a terminal (Termux or Linux).

lessons.title: Lesson 1 — What Is Clio?
lessons.description: Install Clio and understand what it does on your phone or laptop.
lessons.content:
Lesson 1 — What Is Clio?

Welcome to your first lesson on Clio, your intelligent terminal assistant designed to make command-line interactions simpler and more intuitive, especially on your mobile device. Navigating the command line on a phone can be challenging due to smaller screens and virtual keyboards. Clio bridges this gap by letting you use natural language to find and execute shell commands, turning your Termux terminal into a powerful, accessible tool.

What Clio Does for You

Clio is an offline-first CLI assistant that translates your natural language queries into precise shell commands. Instead of memorizing complex syntax like tar -xzvf or df -h, you simply type what you want to achieve in plain English. Clio then suggests the correct command, giving you full control before anything runs.

Here's why Clio is an essential tool for students and developers, particularly when working on Termux on Android:

  • Offline-First Efficiency: Common tasks and command matches are available instantly, even without an internet connection, ensuring your workflow isn't interrupted.
  • Natural Language Understanding: Clio understands casual phrasing, making it incredibly user-friendly. This includes diverse linguistic styles, such as Nigerian Pidgin, ensuring a broad range of users can communicate effectively with it. (Note: All lesson prose will remain in standard English.)
  • Optimized for Termux: Built with Termux on Android in mind, Clio operates with low memory consumption and high stability, preventing crashes and ensuring a smooth experience on your mobile device.
  • User Control: Clio always shows you the suggested command before executing it, asking for your confirmation. This transparent approach means you always know what's happening in your terminal.

Installation on Termux or Linux

Getting Clio up and running is straightforward. Open your Termux app or any Linux terminal and follow these steps:

$ curl -fsSL https://clipilot.themobileprof.com/clio | sh

This command downloads and installs Clio. Once the installation is complete, you can start Clio by simply typing:

$ clio

You should then see a welcome message followed by Clio's distinctive prompt: >>. This prompt indicates that Clio is ready to receive your natural language queries.

💡 Tip
The >> prompt is where you'll interact with Clio. Think of it as a conversation starter. You ask a question, and Clio provides a shell command.

Your First Queries with Clio

Let's try some basic interactions. At the >> prompt, ask Clio to perform common terminal tasks. Remember, you can use everyday language.

>> list files in this folder
SHELL COMMAND: ls
Do you want to run this command? (y/n/m/e/c/h)

Clio will present a suggested command (ls in this case) and prompt you for confirmation. You can type y to run it, n to cancel, or explore other options. You'll notice Clio categorizes its suggestions with headers like SHELL COMMAND, AUTOMATION MODULE, or SETUP WIZARD, especially useful for its Lite profile on Termux.

Try these other examples:

>> check disk space
SHELL COMMAND: df -h
Do you want to run this command? (y/n/m/e/c/h)

>> what is my current directory
SHELL COMMAND: pwd
Do you want to run this command? (y/n/m/e/c/h)

Beyond Basic Commands: Setup Wizards and Automation

Clio is more than just a command finder. It also features powerful Setup Wizards and Automation Modules to streamline your development environment.

  • SETUP WIZARD: These guided processes help you configure common tools. For example, you can set up your Termux environment, Neovim, Git, developer tools, or even a database by typing setup <name> (e.g., setup git). The available wizards are termux, neovim, git, devtools, and database.
  • AUTOMATION MODULE: For repeatable tasks and complex workflows, Clio offers automation modules. You can access these via the modules command or by describing your task in natural language. Modules are downloaded from the CLIPilot registry, and on Termux, you can execute these workflows using clio-run-module.

Clio's ability to understand casual phrasing extends to these advanced features as well. For instance, you could ask:

>> Abeg, how I go see my files for here?
SHELL COMMAND: ls
Do you want to run this command? (y/n/m/e/c/h)

Even with such phrasing, Clio accurately identifies the intent and provides the correct standard English shell command. This capability makes Clio incredibly versatile and user-friendly for a global audience.

Try it now

1

Install Clio

Open your Termux app or Linux terminal and paste the installation command: curl -fsSL https://clipilot.themobileprof.com/clio | sh. Press Enter and wait for it to complete.

2

Start Clio

Once installed, type clio and press Enter. You should see the welcome message and the >> prompt.

3

Ask a Question

At the >> prompt, type "show me running processes" or "what's my IP address?" and press Enter. Observe how Clio suggests a command and waits for your confirmation.

Key Takeaway

Clio is fundamentally a powerful command finder and workflow assistant, not a conversational chatbot that runs arbitrary code. It empowers you by demystifying the command line, offering guided setups, and automating routine tasks, all while keeping you in full control of your terminal environment.

Checklist

  • Clio is installed and launches successfully.
  • You have asked at least one question in plain English at the >> prompt.
  • You have seen Clio's suggested command and the confirm-before-run menu.

lessons.title: Lesson 2 — Ask in Plain English
lessons.description: Use natural language and full sentences to find shell commands.
lessons.content:
Lesson 2 — Ask in Plain English

Welcome back! In the previous lesson, you installed Clio and got familiar with its REPL. Now, let's unlock Clio's most powerful feature: understanding you. On a mobile device, typing exact commands can be cumbersome and prone to typos. Clio simplifies this by letting you use everyday language, turning your natural questions into precise shell commands or guiding you through complex tasks. This means less memorization and more doing, right from your phone.

Clio matches your intent, not exact syntax.

Forget trying to remember obscure flags or the precise order of arguments. Clio is an offline-first CLI assistant designed to interpret what you want to achieve, even if your phrasing isn't perfect. It's like having a seasoned Linux expert right in your terminal, always ready to translate your thoughts into actionable commands.

Shell Commands: Your Instant Catalog

Clio has an extensive, built-in catalog of common Linux commands. When you ask a question related to a standard shell operation, Clio quickly identifies the most relevant command. This is incredibly useful for quickly recalling commands you might use infrequently or discovering new ones.

Here are some examples of how your natural language queries map directly to powerful shell commands:

You type Clio suggests
list files ls
check disk space df -h
find large files find . -type f -size +100M
copy file cp
check memory free -h

Full Sentences Work

You don't need to reduce your questions to keywords. Clio is designed to understand complete sentences, making your interaction feel more natural and intuitive. The more descriptive you are, the better Clio can narrow down the perfect command for your situation. 

>> how do I see which processes are running
ps aux
>> I want to extract a zip file
unzip filename.zip
>> show me files modified in the last week
find . -type f -mtime -7

Casual Phrasing and Local Dialects

Clio goes a step further by understanding informal language. This means you can phrase your questions in a way that feels most comfortable to you, without worrying about formal syntax. This capability extends to various dialects, including Nigerian Pidgin, making Clio truly accessible and user-friendly for a diverse audience. 

>> wetin dey inside this folder
ls -la
>> abeg help me check memory
free -h

While the lesson prose remains in standard English, this feature highlights Clio's commitment to understanding users from different linguistic backgrounds.

💡 Tip
When you're unsure how to phrase a query, try thinking about what you would ask another human. Clio's natural language processing is robust, so don't be afraid to use full sentences or even slightly informal language.

The Result Menu: Your Next Steps

After Clio processes your natural language query, it presents a menu of options. This menu allows you to review the suggested command, see examples, or refine your search. It's an important safety net, ensuring you always understand what Clio is about to do.

  • Show examples: See common flags and usage patterns for the suggested command. This is excellent for learning and customizing.
  • Run the command: Execute the suggested command directly in your terminal after your confirmation.
  • Search again: If the suggestion isn't quite right, you can rephrase your question and try another search.

Always read the command carefully before confirming its execution. This habit ensures you maintain control over your system.

Match Types: Understanding Clio's Suggestions

Clio categorizes its responses to help you understand the nature of the suggestion. These categories are clearly displayed in the header of the result menu, guiding you on whether you're about to run a simple command, a complex workflow, or a setup process.

  • ⌨️ SHELL COMMAND: These are direct Linux commands that Clio suggests based on your query. They run instantly in your terminal.
  • 📦 AUTOMATION MODULE: These represent repeatable tasks or workflows. Clio can suggest these when your request implies a more complex, multi-step operation. You'll learn more about these in Lesson 4.
  • ⭐ SETUP WIZARD: If your query is about installing or configuring a tool (like Neovim, Git, or a database), Clio will suggest a Setup Wizard. These interactive guides streamline complex installations. We'll dive into Setup Wizards in Lesson 3.

Practice: Ask in Plain English

1

Open Clio

If you're not already in Clio's REPL, type clio in your Termux terminal and press Enter to start.

$ clio
>>
2

Ask Five Questions

Experiment by asking Clio five different questions using natural language. Try various phrasings. For instance:

  • "How do I create a new directory?"
  • "What's my IP address?"
  • "I need to install Git."
  • "Show me how to update packages."
  • "Can you help me compress a file?"
3

Note the Match Type

For each question, observe the header that Clio displays (e.g., "⌨️ SHELL COMMAND," "📦 AUTOMATION MODULE," or "⭐ SETUP WIZARD"). This helps you understand how Clio categorizes your intent.

Key Takeaways from This Lesson:

  • Clio understands natural language, including full sentences and casual phrasing.
  • It translates your intent into precise shell commands, automation modules, or setup wizards.
  • The result menu provides options to view examples, run the command, or search again.
  • Always review suggested commands before execution.
  • Clio's match types (SHELL COMMAND, AUTOMATION MODULE, SETUP WIZARD) guide your interaction.

lessons.title: Lesson 3 — Setup Wizards
lessons.description: Use first-class setup wizards to configure Termux, Vim, Git, languages, and databases.
lessons.content:
Welcome to Lesson 3 in your journey with Clio! If you've ever tried to set up a robust development environment directly on your Android phone using Termux, you know it can be a detailed and often time-consuming process. Clio’s Setup Wizards are specifically designed to simplify this, transforming your mobile device into a powerful, ready-to-code workstation with just a few natural language commands. This lesson will guide you through using these wizards to get your environment configured quickly and efficiently.

What are Setup Wizards?

Clio's Setup Wizards are specialized tools for installing and configuring essential development components and your environment. Think of them as guided installers that handle the complexities of setting up tools like Git, Neovim, various programming languages, and databases. They are typically run once to establish your initial setup or to add new capabilities to your Termux environment.

It's important to understand that Setup Wizards are distinct from Clio's Automation Modules (which we'll cover in Lesson 4). While wizards focus on initial configuration, automation modules are for repeatable tasks and workflows.

How to Access Setup Wizards

You can access the full list of available wizards by simply typing setup at Clio's REPL prompt. If you already know which wizard you need, you can invoke it directly by its name. 

>> setup

To launch a specific wizard, just add its name after setup: 

>> setup termux
>> setup neovim
>> setup git

Clio also understands natural language, so you can phrase your request casually, and it will intelligently match it to the appropriate wizard. 

>> configure my dev environment
⭐ [SETUP WIZARD]
Running setup wizard: devtools

>> install git and gh
⭐ [SETUP WIZARD]
Running setup wizard: git

>> setup neovim
⭐ [SETUP WIZARD]
Running setup wizard: neovim

Available Wizards

Clio provides several first-class setup wizards to cover your core development needs on Termux. Each wizard is designed to streamline a specific aspect of your environment configuration.

Wizard Command Purpose
setup termux Sets up a full phone development environment, including Zsh shell, storage permissions, and essential utilities for a smooth Termux experience.
setup neovim Configures Neovim with a small plugin set for generating code, rewriting a selection, finding files.
setup git Guides you through setting up your Git identity and installing the GitHub CLI (gh) for seamless version control.
setup devtools Allows you to pick and install common programming languages and their toolchains, such as Python, Node.js, Go, PHP, or Rust.
setup database Helps you choose and install popular databases like PostgreSQL, MariaDB, Redis, or SQLite for your projects.

How Wizards Run on Termux

When you invoke a setup wizard, Clio doesn't run the entire setup process itself. Instead, it downloads a specific module from the CLIPilot registry the first time it's needed. This module is then executed via a helper script called clio-run-module. This ensures that the setup logic is always up-to-date and tailored for your Termux environment. 

$ clio-run-module termux_setup setup

You don't typically need to type this command yourself; Clio will prompt you or execute it automatically after matching your request to a wizard.

Identifying a Setup Wizard Match

When Clio successfully identifies your request as a Setup Wizard task, you'll see a clear indicator in the REPL output: 

>> setup my python environment
⭐ [SETUP WIZARD]
Running setup wizard: devtools

This label confirms that Clio has understood your intention and is preparing to launch the appropriate wizard.

💡 Tip
Clio is designed to understand a wide range of natural language, including casual phrasing. For example, you could even ask in Nigerian Pidgin, "Clio, abeg help me set up my Termux well well." Clio would still understand your intent to run the setup termux wizard, demonstrating its robust language processing capabilities while keeping the lesson content in standard English.

Try it now

1

Explore the Wizards

Open Clio on Termux and type setup at the >> prompt. Read through the list of available wizards and their descriptions. This will give you a good overview of what Clio can configure for you.

>> setup
2

Choose Your First Setup

Pick a wizard that's relevant to your current needs. If you haven't already, setup termux is an excellent starting point to ensure your Termux environment is fully optimized. Alternatively, if you want to start coding in Python, try setup devtools and select Python.

>> setup termux
3

Run the Wizard

After Clio matches your request to a wizard, it will often provide the clio-run-module command. Confirm the execution to begin the setup process. Clio will download the necessary module from the CLIPilot registry and guide you through the configuration steps. Follow the on-screen prompts carefully to complete your setup.

Key Takeaways

  • Setup Wizards are for installing and configuring your development environment on Termux.
  • They are distinct from Automation Modules, focusing on one-time environment setup.
  • Access wizards using setup or directly with setup <name>.
  • Clio understands natural language for invoking wizards, including casual phrasing.
  • Wizards run via clio-run-module scripts, downloading from the CLIPilot registry.
  • Look for the ⭐ [SETUP WIZARD] label to confirm a match.

lessons.title: Lesson 4 — Automation Modules
lessons.description: Download and run repeatable task workflows from the CLIPilot registry.
lessons.content:
Lesson 4 of 7 in "Clio: Your Terminal Assistant"

Lesson 4 — Automation Modules

Summary: Download and run repeatable task workflows from the CLIPilot registry.

Duration: 12 minutes

For many of us, our Android phone is a powerful, always-on computer. Running a Linux environment like Termux transforms it into a mobile workstation. Clio, your offline-first CLI assistant, supercharges this by letting you automate common tasks directly from your terminal, even without an internet connection. This lesson explores Automation Modules, your key to repeatable workflows on the go.

What are Automation Modules?

Automation modules are pre-built, repeatable workflows designed to handle common tasks. Think of them as intelligent scripts that Clio can download and execute for you. Instead of remembering complex shell commands for daily operations, you can simply ask Clio to perform the task or run a specific module.

These modules cover a wide range of functionalities, from basic file management and system checks to more complex development utilities. They are crafted to save you time and reduce errors by standardizing frequent operations.

Setup Wizards vs. Automation Modules

While both setup wizards and automation modules help streamline your workflow, they serve different primary purposes. Understanding their distinction helps you choose the right tool for the job.

Setup Wizards Automation Modules
When Once / occasionally Whenever needed
Purpose Install & configure Do a task
Browse setup modules
Label [SETUP WIZARD] [AUTOMATION]

Setup wizards get your environment ready, while automation modules help you perform tasks within that ready environment.

Exploring Available Modules

Clio provides straightforward commands to browse the available automation modules. You can view them specifically or see the complete catalog including setup wizards.

To see only automation modules, use the modules command:

>> modules
1: copy_file - Copy files from source to destination. [AUTOMATION]
2: check_disk_space - Display current disk usage statistics. [AUTOMATION]
3: backup_directory - Create a compressed backup of a specified directory. [AUTOMATION]
...
To download a module: download <id>
To run a module: clio-run-module <id> setup

If you want to see both setup wizards and automation modules together, categorized for clarity, use the catalog command:

>> catalog
[SETUP WIZARD]
101: termux - Configure Termux for optimal use.
102: neovim - Set up Neovim with a small plugin set.
...
[AUTOMATION]
201: copy_file - Copy files from source to destination.
202: check_disk_space - Display current disk usage statistics.
...
To download a module: download <id>
To run a module: clio-run-module <id> setup

Each entry in the catalog provides a brief description and the commands you'll need to download and run it. Notice the clear labels like [AUTOMATION] and [SETUP WIZARD] to help you distinguish between them.

Downloading and Syncing Modules

Once you've identified a module you want to use, downloading it is simple.

To download a single module, use its ID:

>> download copy_file
Downloading copy_file from CLIPilot registry...
Module 'copy_file' downloaded successfully.

For a more comprehensive update, you can sync your local module registry with the CLIPilot registry. This ensures you have the latest versions and any new modules.

On your Termux Lite profile, the sync command is optimized to fetch only essential modules, keeping your storage lean:

>> sync
Syncing essential modules for Termux Lite profile...
Registry updated. 5 new modules, 2 updated.

If you require the entire catalog of modules, including those not considered essential for the Lite profile, use sync full:

>> sync full
Syncing full module catalog from CLIPilot registry...
Registry updated. 25 new modules, 5 updated.

This allows you to manage your storage and module collection based on your specific needs.

💡 Tip
After downloading a module, remember to use the clio-run-module <id> setup command to execute its workflow. This command is specific to running Clio's automation modules on Termux.

Natural Language Interaction

One of Clio's most powerful features is its ability to understand natural language. You don't always need to know the exact module ID. You can simply describe what you want to do, and Clio will attempt to match your request with an appropriate automation module or shell command.

For example, if you want to check your disk space:

>> check disk space
📦 [AUTOMATION MODULE] check_disk_space
df -h

Or to back up a directory:

>> backup this directory
📦 [AUTOMATION MODULE] backup_directory
tar -czvf backup_$(date +%Y%m%d).tar.gz .

Clio can even understand casual phrasing, including Nigerian Pidgin. This makes it incredibly accessible and user-friendly, allowing you to interact in a way that feels natural to you. However, the lesson prose will remain in standard English.

Here's an example of Clio understanding a Pidgin phrase:

>> wetin be my ip address?
SHELL COMMAND
ip addr show

Notice the 📦 [AUTOMATION MODULE] or SHELL COMMAND header in the output, indicating how Clio interpreted your request.

Try it now

Let's put what you've learned into practice by exploring and running an automation module.

1

Explore Modules

Open your Termux terminal and type >> modules. Browse through the list and identify an automation module that sounds useful or interesting to you. Note down its ID.

>> modules
2

Download and Run

Using the ID you noted, download the module. Then, execute the module using the clio-run-module command. Observe the output and see how the module performs its task.

>> download <module_id>
>> clio-run-module <module_id> setup

Replace <module_id> with the actual ID you chose.

Key Takeaways

By completing this lesson, you should now understand:

  • The purpose of Clio's Automation Modules for repeatable tasks.
  • How Automation Modules differ from Setup Wizards.
  • How to browse available modules using modules and catalog.
  • The process of downloading individual modules with download <id>.
  • How to sync modules, including sync for essential modules on Termux Lite and sync full for the complete catalog.
  • Clio's capability to understand natural language, including casual phrasing, to match commands or modules.
  • How to run a downloaded module using clio-run-module <id> setup.

Automation modules empower you to streamline your mobile terminal workflow, making complex tasks simpler and faster. Continue to the next lesson to deepen your understanding of Clio's capabilities!

lessons.title: Lesson 5 — Offline Mode & Sync
lessons.description: Understand lite profile, layers, and when you need internet.
lessons.content:
Lesson 5 — Offline Mode & Sync

Summary: Understand lite profile, layers, and when you need internet.

Clio is designed with an offline-first philosophy, making it an incredibly powerful tool for your mobile device, especially on Termux. On a phone, reliable internet access isn't always a given. Whether you're commuting through a tunnel, in a remote area, or simply trying to conserve data, Clio ensures that your essential shell commands and setup wizards are always at your fingertips, even without a network connection.

Most common queries and tasks with Clio never require an internet connection, providing instant responses and uninterrupted productivity wherever you are.

Clio's Detection Layers (Simplified)

Clio processes your natural language queries through several layers, prioritizing local resources to deliver speed and reliability:

  • Phrase & Catalog: This is the fastest layer. Clio's core binary includes a vast internal catalog of common commands and phrases, allowing for instant, network-free responses to many questions.
  • Man Pages: Clio can search local manual pages installed on your system to find relevant commands and usage information. Note: This layer is often skipped on a lite profile to conserve resources.
  • Automation Modules: If a query matches an automation module, Clio checks its local SQLite cache. If the module is already downloaded, it can execute the task offline.
  • Remote Search: Only if all local layers fail to find a suitable match will Clio attempt to query the CLIPilot API over the internet. This ensures you get the most comprehensive assistance when needed, but only as a last resort.

Lite Profile for Termux/Android

On devices like phones running Termux, Clio often operates in a lite profile. This profile is optimized for environments with limited memory and storage, ensuring Clio runs smoothly without consuming excessive resources.

  • In lite mode, Clio has a smaller memory footprint.
  • The sync command downloads only the most essential automation modules to your device. This keeps your local storage lean.
  • If you require access to the full range of automation modules from the CLIPilot registry, you can explicitly use sync full when you have an internet connection.

You can review and modify Clio's profile settings in its configuration file, located at ~/.clio/config.yaml:

profile: auto # auto | lite | full remote_search: auto
💡 Tip
If you're unsure which profile Clio is using, check your ~/.clio/config.yaml file. Setting profile: auto allows Clio to intelligently select the best profile based on your system's resources, often defaulting to lite on Termux.

When You Need an Internet Connection

While Clio excels offline, there are specific scenarios where an internet connection is necessary:

  • Initial Installation: Installing Clio itself requires fetching the script via curl -fsSL https://clipilot.themobileprof.com/clio | sh.
  • First-Time Module Downloads: When you use download <id>, run sync (or sync full), or initiate a setup wizard (e.g., setup git), Clio needs to download the relevant automation modules from the CLIPilot registry. Once downloaded, they are cached locally for offline use.
  • Remote Search: If your natural language query cannot be resolved by any of Clio's local detection layers (phrase & catalog, man pages, local modules), Clio will attempt a remote search via the CLIPilot API.

Local Storage

Clio manages its local data efficiently on your device:

  • Database: All cached automation modules and other operational data are stored in ~/.clio/clio.db.
  • Configuration: Your personal settings for Clio are kept in ~/.clio/config.yaml.

Try it now

Let's experience Clio's offline capabilities firsthand:

1

Go Offline and Ask

Turn off your device's Wi-Fi and mobile data. Now, open Termux, launch Clio with clio, and try asking a few common questions. Notice how Clio responds instantly.

>> how I go install git for my phone?
SHELL COMMAND: pkg install git

Even with casual phrasing or Nigerian Pidgin, Clio understands and provides the correct shell command, all without an internet connection!

2

Sync Up

Reconnect to the internet. Then, run the sync command in Clio. This will update your local cache of essential automation modules, ensuring you have the latest versions available for offline use.

>> sync
Syncing essential modules...
Modules updated successfully.

Key Takeaways

By understanding Clio's offline-first design and sync mechanisms, you can maximize its utility on your mobile device:

  • Clio prioritizes local resources for speed and reliability.
  • The lite profile on Termux optimizes performance for mobile environments.
  • Most common commands and queries work perfectly offline.
  • Internet is needed for initial setup, first-time module downloads, and remote searches.
  • Regularly sync to keep your local automation modules updated for offline use.

lessons.title: Lesson 6 — Termux on Android
lessons.description: Phone-specific tips: install, clio-run-module, storage, and 32-bit devices.
lessons.content:
Lesson 6 — Termux on Android

Clio is designed to empower students coding on their phone, transforming your Android device into a powerful development environment. With Clio on Termux, you gain an intelligent assistant that understands your natural language queries, helping you manage your system, execute commands, and automate tasks directly from your pocket.

Install on Termux

Getting Clio up and running on Termux is straightforward. First, ensure you have curl installed, which is essential for downloading the Clio installer script. Once curl is ready, you can fetch and run the installer in a single command.

💡 Tip
Before installing, it's a good practice to update your Termux packages. Run pkg update && pkg upgrade to ensure all your system packages are up-to-date. This can prevent potential conflicts during installation. 
$ pkg install curl
$ curl -fsSL https://clipilot.themobileprof.com/clio | sh

The installer script automatically detects your device's architecture and places the clio executable and the clio-run-module helper script into your $PREFIX/bin/ directory, making them immediately accessible from your Termux prompt.

Why clio-run-module Exists

Android's security model imposes certain restrictions on Go binaries, including Clio, by blocking some system calls. To ensure full functionality and seamless execution of complex workflows, Clio leverages a special helper script: clio-run-module.

This helper script acts as a bridge, allowing automation modules to run their workflows via a standard bash shell, bypassing the Go binary restrictions. This design ensures that your automation tasks, from system setup to development tooling, execute reliably on Termux.

>> setup termux
SHELL COMMAND: clio-run-module termux_setup setup

When Clio suggests an automation module, it will automatically use clio-run-module. You should never manually paste module YAML into your terminal; always let Clio handle the download and execution from the CLIPilot registry.

First-Run Path: Getting Started

Once Clio is installed, a few simple steps will get you ready to unlock its full potential on your Android device.

Try it now

1

Install Clio

Follow the installation steps above to get Clio on your Termux environment.

2

Launch Clio

Type clio at your Termux prompt to enter the REPL (Read-Eval-Print Loop) interface.

3

Complete Setup Wizard

Run the setup termux command (or simply setup) to initiate the Termux-specific wizard. This wizard will configure essential features like storage access.

4

Synchronize Modules

If you are online, run sync to download the latest automation modules and updates from the CLIPilot registry. This ensures Clio has access to the most current capabilities. You can also use sync full for a complete refresh.

5

Start Asking Questions

You're all set! Begin interacting with Clio using natural language to perform tasks, get information, or set up development tools. Type help for assistance or exit to leave the REPL.

32-bit vs. 64-bit Phones

Clio is designed to be compatible with a wide range of Android devices. For older phones that utilize a 32-bit architecture (often identified as armv7l), the installer script automatically detects this and downloads the appropriate arm binary. For newer 64-bit devices (armv8l), the arm64 binary is installed. This automatic detection ensures optimal performance and compatibility without requiring manual intervention from the user.

Storage Access on Termux

Accessing your phone's shared storage, such as your Downloads folder or external SD card, is crucial for many development tasks. The setup termux wizard includes a step to configure storage access by running termux-setup-storage.

Once completed, you will find a convenient symbolic link to your shared storage at ~/storage/ within your Termux home directory. This allows Clio and your scripts to seamlessly interact with files stored elsewhere on your Android device.

Natural Language on Your Phone

Clio's core strength is its ability to understand natural language, and this capability functions identically on Termux. You can phrase your requests in plain English, just as you would speak to a human assistant.

Clio is also designed to understand casual phrasing, including regional dialects like Nigerian Pidgin, making it highly accessible and user-friendly for a diverse range of users. The lesson content remains in standard English, but Clio's understanding is flexible.

>> list files in downloads folder
SHELL COMMAND: ls ~/storage/downloads
>> check disk space
SHELL COMMAND: df -h
>> Wetin dey my downloads folder?
SHELL COMMAND: ls ~/storage/downloads

Troubleshooting Common Issues

Even with a smooth setup, you might encounter minor hurdles. Here's a quick guide to common problems and their solutions:

Problem Fix
clio-run-module: not found This usually means the installation was incomplete or the executable path is not correctly set. Re-run the Clio install script: curl -fsSL https://clipilot.themobileprof.com/clio | sh.
Module not found or outdated Clio needs to retrieve the latest module definitions. Run sync to update your local module registry. If you know the specific module ID, you can also use download <id>. You can also view available modules with the modules or catalog commands.
No match offline / Limited results Clio is offline-first, but for the widest range of matches, especially for new or complex queries, an internet connection is beneficial for remote search. Rephrase your query or ensure you are online for a broader search.

Practice Your Skills

The best way to learn is by doing! Take a moment to interact with Clio on your Termux setup.

Practice now

1

Verify Termux Setup

If you haven't already, run setup termux within Clio to ensure all Termux-specific configurations are applied. If you have, simply confirm its completion.

2

Ask Three Queries

Experiment with three different natural language queries. Try asking for system information, file management tasks, or even basic development commands. For example:

  • "How much free space do I have?"
  • "Show me my current directory"
  • "Create a new folder called 'my_project'"
3

Explore Modules

Type modules to see a list of available automation modules, or catalog to browse the CLIPilot registry. You can then use download <id> to get a specific module.

Key Takeaways for Clio on Termux

  • Clio transforms your Android phone into a powerful, natural-language-driven development tool.
  • The installer automatically handles 32-bit and 64-bit device compatibility.
  • clio-run-module is essential for executing automation workflows due to Android's Go binary restrictions.
  • The setup termux wizard configures vital features like storage access at ~/storage/.
  • Clio understands diverse natural language phrasing, including casual speech.
  • Regularly sync to keep your automation modules up-to-date from the CLIPilot registry.

lessons.content:
Lesson 7 — Practice & Next Steps

Congratulations on reaching the final lesson in our "Clio: Your Terminal Assistant" series! Throughout these lessons, you've learned how to leverage Clio's natural language capabilities to streamline your workflow on Termux and Android. Its offline-first design is particularly valuable on mobile, ensuring you have a powerful assistant for shell commands, automation, and system setup, even when connectivity is limited.

This lesson is designed to solidify your understanding through practical challenges, provide a handy command reference, and guide you on where to go next. Embrace the power of asking questions in plain English, and let Clio translate your intent into precise shell actions.

Capstone Challenges

Now it's time to put your skills to the test! Complete these challenges using Clio's natural language interface. Try to formulate your questions without looking up the exact shell commands first. This will help you build intuition for how Clio interprets your requests.

Try it now

1

Files Challenge

Ask Clio to "show hidden files with details in this folder". Observe the command Clio suggests and its output. This covers basic file system navigation and listing.

>> show hidden files with details in this folder
ls -la
2

Space Challenge

Inquire about your device's storage by asking Clio to "check how much disk space is left". This is crucial for managing resources on your mobile device.

3

Search Challenge

Challenge Clio to "find files larger than 50 megabytes". This demonstrates Clio's ability to handle more complex queries involving file attributes.

4

Setup Wizard Exploration

Run one setup wizard you have not tried yet. First, type setup to see the available wizards, then pick one like setup git or setup devtools to experience how Clio guides you through complex configurations.

>> setup
SHELL COMMAND / AUTOMATION MODULE / SETUP WIZARD
    termux: Basic Termux environment setup
    neovim: Configure Neovim for development
    git: Initialize Git and configure user
    devtools: Install common development tools
    database: Setup a local database server
>> setup git
# Clio will guide you through Git setup...
5

Automation Module Experience

Browse the available automation modules by typing modules. Download one that interests you using download <id>, then read its description. Remember, on Termux, you'd use clio-run-module to execute a downloaded module's workflow.

Quick Command Reference

Here's a concise list of Clio's core commands to help you navigate its features efficiently. Keep this handy for quick lookups.

Goal Clio command
List all setup wizards setup
List all automation modules modules
List both wizards and modules catalog
Download a specific module download <id>
Sync local registry with CLIPilot sync
Perform a full sync (including updates) sync full
Access built-in help help
Exit Clio REPL exit

When Clio Cannot Match

Clio is powerful, but sometimes your phrasing might not immediately match its understanding. If Clio struggles to provide a relevant command, don't worry! Try these strategies:

  • Rephrase More Simply: Break down complex requests into simpler verb + noun phrases, such as "list files" instead of "show me all the files in this directory with their sizes."
  • Check the Catalog: Use the catalog command to see the full list of available setup wizards and automation modules. This can give you ideas for what Clio is designed to handle.
  • Explicit Setup: For setup tasks, try setup <name> explicitly (e.g., setup neovim) if your natural language query isn't working.
  • Verify Connectivity: If you expect a match from the CLIPilot registry (for new modules or updates), ensure your device has an active internet connection.
💡 Tip

Clio is designed to understand a wide range of natural language, including casual phrasing and even Nigerian Pidgin. While this lesson uses standard English, feel free to experiment with how you phrase your questions in your own interactions. Clio will do its best to interpret your intent.

>> Abeg, wetin be my IP address?
ip addr show

This capability helps make Clio accessible and intuitive for a broader audience, reducing the barrier to entry for terminal usage.

Keep Learning

Your journey with Clio doesn't end here! The world of terminal automation and development is vast, and Clio is your constant companion. Here are some ways to continue expanding your knowledge and capabilities:

  • CLIPilot Registry: New automation modules are regularly added to the CLIPilot registry. Remember to run sync or sync full periodically to update your local Clio instance with the latest additions.
  • GitHub Repository: Explore the Clio project on GitHub at github.com/themobileprof/clio. You can contribute, report issues, or simply learn more about its inner workings.
  • TheMobileProf Courses: Enhance your foundational knowledge by combining Clio with other micro-courses from TheMobileProf, especially those focused on Linux fundamentals and Git version control. This will deepen your understanding of the commands Clio executes.

You Finished When…

You've successfully completed this series and are ready to leverage Clio effectively when you can confidently say:

  • I can install and launch Clio on Termux or Linux.
  • I can distinguish between setup wizards and automation modules.
  • I can download and run at least one automation module.
  • I can ask questions in plain English and confidently expect Clio to assist me.

Stop Googling. Start asking.
